title: SA/26/2007 of CHINTAMANI PATHAK Vs M/S KESAR ENTERPRISES LTD. BAHERI, DISTRICT BAREILLY. THROUGH ITS PRESIDENT H.H. MALIK.

paras.text:
IN THE HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND
AT NAINITAL
Second Appeal No. 26 of 2007
Chintamani Pathak ......Appellant
Versus
M/s Kesar Enterprises Ltd. ......Respondent
Present:
Mr. Rajendra Dobhal, the learned Senior Advocate assisted by
Mr. Shubhang Dobhal for the appellant.
Mr. B.P.S. Mer, the learned counsel for the respondent.
Date of hearing: 29.08.2022
Date of judgement: 21.09.2022
Sri S.K. Mishra, J.
Upon hearing the learned counsel for the parties, this Court made the
following judgment:
This second appeal, filed under Section 100 of
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (hereinafter referred to
as the Code for brevity), was admitted on 10.08.2017,
for answering the following substantial question of
law:-
(i) Whether the lower appellate court has erred
in law in allowing the appeal and upsetting the
judgment and decree of the trial court without
reversing the finding of the trial court and giving
any independent finding on any of the issues and
without framing any points for determination as
is required under Order 41 Rule 31.
2. The additional questions as hereinunder also arise
during hearing of the appeal. They are enumerated
below:-
(ii) Is suit not maintainable as there has been
non compliance of Order 29 Rule 1 of the Code

2
as the plaint has not been verified by authorized
Director of the Company?
(iii) Whether the plaintiff/respondent is not the
owner of the property in question as it has been
recorded in the name of one Jeevan Lal and not
in the name of the Company?
3. It may be stated here that a suit was filed by the
plaintiff/respondent before the Civil Judge (J.D)
Rudrapur, District Udham Singh Nagar bearing Civil Suit
No. 46 of 2001,which was dismissed on contest vide
judgment dated 25.07.2005. The plaintiff/respondent
preferred an appeal to the court of the learned District
Judge, Udham Singh Nagar, at Rudrapur, which was
registered as Civil Appeal No. 71 of 2005. As per the
judgment dated 20.12.2006, the appeal was allowed.
The decision of the Civil Judge (J.D) Rudrapur, was set
aside and a decree for recovery of possession passed in
favour of the plaintiff/respondent. Such judgment of
the appellate court is challenged in this case.
4. The plaintiff/respondent M/s Kesar Enterprises is a
registered company under the Companies Act, 1956.
Mr. S.S. Bhatia was the Vice President of the company
as well as power of attorney holder and was competent
to file civil proceedings on behalf of the company. The
plaintiff/respondent as an industrial unit, engaged in
production of sugar and distillery. It had office in
Udham Singh Nagar since 1983. It has a Research and
Development Unit Khurpia Firm at Tehsil Kichha and for

3
the purpose of imparting education to children of it
employees, it established a school. It also constructed
quarters for the occupation of the teachers. The
defendant/appellant herein, was the Principal of that
school and in lieu of such services rendered by him, the
appellant was granted the property in question for his
occupation/residence and for that he was paying
nominal rent to the school. The appellant was to vacate
the said quarter after his retirement. However, he did
not return the same after the retirement, hence, the
plaintiff filed suit for eviction. Criminal proceedings
were also initiated against him for trespass but that
case was stayed by the High Court of Allahabad.
5. The short defence that has been taken by the
appellant/defendant is that the plaintiff is not the
rightful owner of the property and he cannot seek
eviction against the defendant. It is further stated that
the land in question was settled in the name of Jeevan
Lal and on his death the land is reverted back to the
State. While considering the pleadings of the parties,
the learned Civil Jude (J.D) Rudrapur, framed six
issues. Issue no. 2 and 3 are most important which
relates to the allotment of the quarters to the
appellant/defendant during his services as a Head
Master of the school and whether his possession
thereon, after his retirement on 14.12.1997 is illegal.
In course of trial, two witnesses were examined on
behalf of each of the parties and the learned Civil Judge
(J.D), after considering the material on records, come

4
to the conclusion that the respondent (appellant herein)
is not rightful owner of the property. He cannot
maintain the suit. However, the learned first appellate
court came to the conclusion that the judgment passed
by the learned Civil Judge (J.D) is not proper and
requires interference and there is a contradiction in the
findings on issue no. 1 and 4 by the learned Trial
Judge.
6. Before proceeding to deal with the substantial
questions mentioned above, this Court take note of
certain undisputed facts. Firstly, there is no dispute that
the appellant was working as Head Master of the
school, which is being run by the plaintiff/respondent
and that in lieu of his services rendered as Head Master
of the school, which was setup for the betterment of
the children of the employees of the company; that the
appellant was given the possession of the quarter on
nominal rent in lieu of his services. This fact is not
disputed by Mr. Rajendra Dobhal, the learned Senior
Advocate appearing for the appellant. Such facts are
also apparent from the evidence of the appellant
himself that the quarter was given to him in lieu of his
services. Secondly, it is not disputed that Jeevan Lal
was an agent of the company and the land was
recorded in the name of Jeevan Lal as a representative
of the company and not in his name or individual
capacity.

5
7. Coming to the question at hand, the learned
Senior Advocate appearing for the appellant would rely
upon a recent decided case by the Hon'ble Supreme
Court in Civil Appeal No.(s) 1117 of 2009 Somakka
(Dead) by LRs. Vs. K.P. Basavaraj (Dead) by LRs.
Decided on 13.06.2022, wherein the Hon'ble Supreme
Court has set aside the order of High Court holding that
it committed serious error in neither forming the point
of determination nor considering the evidence on
record, in particular which had been relied upon by the
Trial Court, and, therefore, the Hon'ble Supreme Court
has set aside the judgment of the first appellate court
i.e. High Court of Karanataka.
8. Order 41 Rule 31 of the Code provide for the
content, date and signature of the judgment, which
reads as follows:-
31. Contents, date and signature of judgment.- The
judgment of the Appellate Court shall be in writing
and shall state-
(a) the points for determination;
(b) the decision thereon;
(c) where the decree appealed from is reversed
or varied, the relief to which the appellant is
entitled,
And shall at the time that it is pronounced be signed
and dated by the Judge or by the Judges concurring
therein.
9. In the case of G. Amalorpavam & Ors. vs. R.C.
Diocese of Madurai & Ors., (2006) 3 SCC 224, the
Hon'ble Supreme Court while sitting in appeal over the
judgment of Madras High Court, dismissing the second
appeal of the appellant under Section 100 of the Code

6
had considered the effect and purport of Order 41 Rule
31 of the Code. The Hon'ble Supreme Court has also
held that the question whether in a particular case
there has been substantial compliance with the
provisions of Order 41 Rule 31 of the Code has to be
determined on the nature of the judgment delivered in
each case. It further held that non compliance of the
provisions may vitiate the judgment and make it wholly
void, and may be ignored if there has been substantial
compliance with it and the second appellate court is in
a position to ascertain the findings of the lower
appellate court. The Hon'ble Supreme Court has further
held that it is no doubt desirable that the appellate
court should comply with all the requirements of Order
41 Rule 31 of the Code, but if it is possible to make out
from the judgment that there is substantial compliance
with the said requirement and justice has not thereby
suffered, that would be sufficient. It is further held that
the highest Court of the Country that has considered
the entire evidence on record and discussed the same
in detail, came to the conclusion that the appellate
court's findings are supported by reasons even though
the point has not been framed by the appellate court
there is substantial compliance of the aforesaid
provisions and the judgment is not in any manner
vitiated by the absence of a point of determination.
Where there is an endeavour on the part of the first
appellate court to consider the controversy between the
parties and there is proper appraisement of the
respective cases and weighing and balancing of the

7
evidence, facts and the other considerations appearing
on both sides is clearly manifest by the perusal of the
judgment of the lower appellate court, it would be a
valid judgment even though it does not contain the
points of determination. The Hon'ble Supreme Court
further held that the object of rule in making it
incumbent upon the appellate court to frame points for
determination and to cite reasons for the decision is to
focus attention of the court on the rival contentions
which arise for determination and also to provide
litigating parties opportunity in understanding the
ground upon which the decision is founded with a view
to enable them to know the basis of the decision and if
so considered appropriate and so advised to avail the
remedy of second appeal conferred by Section 100 of
the Code.
10. The aforesaid judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme
Court has been twice followed by the Co-ordinate Bench
of this Court. In the case of Girvar Lal vs. Neena
Rajdan, 2012 SCC online UTT 309, the Co-ordinate
Bench after taking into consideration the facts of the
reported case as well as the law governing the field has
held that if there is substantial compliance of order 41
Rule 31 of the Code, the judgment of the first appellate
court should not be set aside on technical shortcomings
in the judgment. The same view is taken in the case of
Vinod Kumar vs. Mandir Laxmi Narayan &Ors., 2020
SCC online UTT 119.

8
11. In applying these principles to the case at hand
this Court finds that though the judgment of the
learned District Judge, Udham Singh Nagar is short
one, it is right on the point and he has not ignored any
material available on record. The short question that
was agitated before him is that the respondent is not
the owner of the property and that it cannot maintain a
suit for recovery of possession. This issue has been
very correctly decided by the learned first appellate
judge and only because it has not delineated in a
separate paragraph regarding the point of
determination, the judgment cannot be set aside.
Moreover, it is seen that in the judgment itself the
learned first appellate judge has considered and
reflected the issues that were framed by the learned
Civil Judge (J.D) being the court of first instance, and,
therefore, it cannot be said that the real controversy
between the party was not clear before the parties and
their respective learned counsels appearing before the
first appellate court.
12. Moreover, in a case where substantial justice has
been done, the courts should not on technical grounds
set aside the judgment and remand the case only for
the purpose of framing the points of determination and
rewriting the judgment. It would be a futile exercise. It
is time and again stated and reiterated by the Hon'ble
Supreme Court as well as by the various High Courts in
India that whenever substantial question of law is
pitted against a procedural aspect of law then the court

9
must remember that procedural law is the hand maid of
substantive justice and substantive justice should
always be preferred over the procedural law. In this
case, the appellant does not claim that the property
belongs to him, even if his case is accepted, then the
property which considered a piece of land and quarters
standing thereon would be belonging to the State and
the State, if the case of the appellant is taken to be
correct, would be the owner of the land whereas the
houses i.e. quarters constructed thereon, so
constructed by the respondent/company would be it
property. Thus the suit cannot be dismissed on the
ground that defendant has a better title then the
plaintiff, in fact the defendant does not plead that he
has title over the property and, in fact, he has no title
over the property in question. He is taking a technical
plea that the respondent/company cannot maintain a
suit for eviction.
13. In this connection we take note of Section 116 of
the Indian Evidence Act, which reads as follows:-
116. Estoppel of tenant; and of licensee of person in
possession.-No tenant of immovable property, or
person claiming through such tenant, shall, during
the continuance of the tenancy, be permitted to deny
that the landlord of such tenant had, at the
beginning of the tenancy, a title to such immovable
property; and no person who came upon any
immovable property by the licence of the person in
possession thereof, shall be permitted to deny that

10
such person had a title to such possession at the
time when such licence was given.
Interpreting the same, the Hon'ble Supreme Court
in the case of Bansraj Laltaprasad Mishra vs. Stanley
Parker Jones, (2006) 3 SCC 9113 has held that a
person who has been granted license or permission to
hold the property by the landlord or by the original
owner cannot challenge the title of the property later
on. Thus, the case of the appellant in this case is
barred by Section 116 of the Evidence Act, which is
estoppel against the tenant or the licensee. Thus, on
this substantial question of law the appellant's case is
not acceptable and it cannot be held that he shall be
allowed to possess the land even though he has retired
from the post for which the quarter was allotted to him
on superannuation.
Mr. Dobhal, the learned Senior Advocate
appearing did not dispute that the appellant was the
Head Master of the school in question and was allotted
the said quarter in lieu of his services as the Head
Master of the school. He cannot at this stage challenge
the title of the respondents.
14. The second substantial question of law is
regarding non compliance of Order 29 Rule 1 of the
Code which provides for verification of pleadings. It is
stated that the pleadings have not been verified by a
competent person representing the company. For the
purpose of appreciation, the same is quoted below-

11
Subscription and verification of pleading. In
suits by or against a corporation, any pleading may
be signed and verified on behalf of the corporation by
the security or by any director or other principal
officer of the corporation who is able to depose to
the facts of the case.
15. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of United
Bank of India vs. Naresh Kumar & Ors., (1996) 6 SCC
660, dealing with the similar question with respect to a
suit filed by the public sector bank has held as follows:-
"9. In cases like the present where suits are instituted or
defended on behalf of a public corporation, public interest
should not be permitted to be defeated on a mere
technicality. Procedural defects which do not go to the root
of the matter should not be permitted to defeat a just
cause. There is sufficient power in the Courts, under the
Code of Civil Procedure, to ensure that injustice is not done
to any party who has a just case. As far as possible a
substantive right should not be allowed to be defeated on
account of a procedural irregularity which is curable.
10. It cannot be disputed that a company like the
appellant can sue and be sued in its own name. Under
Order 6 Rule 14 of the Code of Civil Procedure a pleading is
required to be signed by the party and its pleader, if any.
As a company is a juristic entity it is obvious that some
person has to sign the pleadings on behalf of the company.
Order 29 Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, therefore,
provides that in a suit by against a corporation the
Secretary or any Director or other Principal officer of the
corporation who is able to depose to the facts of the case
might sign and verify on behalf of the company. Reading
Order 6 Rule 14 together with Order 29 Rule 1 of the Code
of Civil Procedure it would appear that even in the absence
of any formal letter of authority or power of attorney
having been executed a person referred to in Rule 1 of
Order 29 can, by virtue of the office which he holds, sign
and verify the pleadings on behalf of the corporation. In
addition thereto and de hors Order 29 Rule 1 of the Code
of Civil Procedure, as a company is a juristic entity, it can
duly authorise any person to sign the plaint or the written
statement on its behalf and this would be regarded as
sufficient compliance with the provisions of Order 6 Rule

12
14 of the Code of Civil Procedure. A person may be
expressly authorised to sign the pleadings on behalf of the
company, for example by the Board of Directors passing a
resolution to that effect or by a power of attorney being
executed in favour of any individual. In absence thereof
and in cases where pleadings have been signed by one of
it's officers a Corporation can ratify the said action of it's
officer in signing the pleadings. Such ratification can be
express or implied. The Court can, on the basis of the
evidence on record, and after taking all the circumstances
of the case, specially with regard to the conduct of the
trial, come to the conclusion that the corporation had
ratified the act of signing of the pleading by it's officer."
16. Thus, it is clear that in certain situation, in public
interest, a strict adherence to the rules of filing of
proceeding, a suit or a writ petition can be relaxed,
especially when the public interest is involved. This
view has been taken by the Orissa High Court in the
case of Jindal Steel & Power Limited & Anr. vs. State of
Orissa, 2020 SCC online ORI 806, AIR 21 Ori 41. Thus,
this Court is of the opinion that in this case, the
pleadings has been verified by the Vice President of the
company who happens to be a Principal Officer. The
defendant has not taken a specific plea in his written
statement that there has been non compliance of the
provisions of the Companies Act in the sense that there
is no resolution of the Board authorising any person to
file or initiate any civil proceedings. Such a defect as is
clear from the aforesaid judgment of the Hon'ble
Supreme Court in the case of United Bank of India
(supra), could have been removed as it is a curable
defect and can be allowed to be removed by at any
point of time keeping in view the public interest.

13
Section 291 of the Companies Act, 1956, provides
general powers of the Board, which are quoted
hereunder.
291. General powers of Board.
(1) Subject to the provisions of this Act, the Board of
directors of a company shall be entitled to exercise
all such powers, and to do all such acts and things,
as the company is authorised to exercise and do:
Provided that the Board shall not exercise any power
or do any act or thing which is directed or required,
whether by this or any other Act or by the
memorandum or articles of the company or
otherwise, to be exercised or done by the company
in general meeting: Provided further that in
exercising any such power or doing any such act or
thing, the Board shall be subject to the provisions
con- tained in that behalf in this or any other Act, or
in the memorandum or articles of the company, or in
any regulations not inconsistent therewith and duly
made thereunder, including regulation made by the
company in general meeting.
(2) No regulation made by the company in general
meeting shall invalidate any prior act of the Board
which would have been valid if that regulation had
not been made.
Though, the litigation is between two private
individual, i.e., company and one of its former
employee, this Court is of the opinion that since
company established a school, and has also constructed
quarters, which is a matter of the dispute, which has
been allotted to the Head Master, who was discharging
his duty then it would be expedient to hold that the
litigation in the ultimate analysis has also an effect of
public interest. If the present Head Master of the school
is not provided with proper accommodation in lieu of
his services that he is rendering to school, i.e., very
noble and important function of imparting teaching to
the students then the future of those students will

14
definitely effected. Hence, this Court is of the view that
there has been substantial compliance of Order 29 Rule
1 of the Code as well as Section 291 of the Companies
Act.
17. Coming to the third question, this Court finds that
land undisputedly was recorded in the name of Jeevan
Lal, reflecting him to be an agent of the company. It is
very emphatically argued by the learned counsel for the
respondent Mr. B.P.S. Mer that land was settled in the
name of the agent of the company. The agent of the
company did not have an independent right. He was
holding land only on behalf of the company and on his
death the company continues to be the owner of the
property and in this case the provisions of UPZA&LR Act
is not applicable, and, therefore, it cannot be said that
after death of the said Jeevan Lal the land will vest with
the State of Uttarakhand.
18. Thus, answering the all questions framed in this
case as above, this Court is of the opinion that there is
no merit in the second appeal and the second appeal
requires to be dismissed. Hence, the second appeal is
dismissed with cost through out.
The appellant shall bear the costs all throughout.
(Sanjaya Kumar Mishra, J.)
PV
